### C-V1R2-03
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Gen 1:1 is among Scripture’s best-known verses, yet translation and meaning are highly contested: absolute independent clause vs dependent temporal clause, and the relation of v. 1 to v. 2 and the rest of the chapter.
- **Quote:** “Among the most well-known passages of Scripture is its very first verse, traditionally translated as above. Nevertheless, no small controversy among biblical scholars has swirled around both the translation and the meaning of the verse. … First, should v. 1 be translated as an independent clause… Or is the verse to be understood as a dependent clause, “When God began to create... ,” … Second, what is the relation of v. 1 to v. 2…”
- **Locus:** raw L2285–L2287 / Gen 1:1
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[genesis]], [[creation-ex-nihilo]], [[genesis-creation-accounts]]

### C-V1R2-04
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Four translation options for *berēʾšîṯ*: (1) absolute, independent clause; (2) indeterminate relative temporal “Initially”; (3) construct subordinated to v. 2; (4) construct subordinated to v. 3 with v. 2 parenthetical. Options (1) and (4) have widest scholarly support; Hebrew competence alone cannot settle the matter.
- **Quote:** “(1) The first word, berē‘šîṯ, is in the absolute state … and all of v. 1 is an independent clause… (2) … “Initially (or first, to start with) God created....” (3) The first word is in the construct state … subordinated to v. 2… (4) … subordinated to v. 3, with v. 2 taken as a parenthesis… A knowledge of the Hebrew language will not be sufficient in itself to settle the matter… interpretations (1) and (4) have by far the widest support.”
- **Locus:** raw L2289–L2291 / Gen 1:1
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[genesis]], [[creation-ex-nihilo]]

### C-V1R2-05
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Arguments for dependent-clause reading include: construct vowels; structural parallel to 2:4b temporal construction; *rēʾšîṯ* almost always construct (except possibly Isa 46:10); and alleged Enuma elish parallel (protasis 1:1 // lines 1–2; parenthesis 1:2 // 3–8; apodosis 1:3 // line 9).
- **Quote:** “The main lines of argument in support of taking v. 1 as a dependent clause which prepares for the main clause in v. 3 are as follows. (a) The vowels in the word berē’ šîṯ indicate the word to be construct… (b) In the “second” Creation account (2:4bff.) the temporal construction is employed… (c) The word rē’ šîṯ occurs some fifty times… except possibly Isa. 46:10… (d) … Babylonian Epic of Creation—the Enuma elish… first nine lines parallel the first two verses of Genesis.”
- **Locus:** raw L2293–L2322 / Gen 1:1–3; cf. 2:4b
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[genesis]], [[genesis-ancient-near-east]], [[genesis-creation-accounts]], [[documentary-hypothesis]]

### C-V1R2-06
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** The absolute vs temporal issue is not “esoteric quibbling”: it decides whether Gen 1:1 teaches absolute beginning as a direct act of God, or affirms matter/chaos prior to creation (one God vs God + preexistent chaos). “Creation of chaos” would be a contradiction in terms.
- **Quote:** “The issue between these two options—“In the beginning when” and “In the beginning”—is not esoteric quibbling… Does Gen. 1:1 teach an absolute beginning of creation as a direct act of God? Or does it affirm the existence of matter before creation of the heavens and the earth? … in the beginning there was one—God; or … two—God and preexistent chaos? … the concept of the creation of chaos would be a contradiction in terms.”
- **Locus:** raw L2327–L2327 / Gen 1:1
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[creation-ex-nihilo]], [[genesis]], [[account-of-creation]]

### C-V1R2-07
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Westermann and others choose traditional translation from wider-chapter theology (repudiation/demythologizing of Enuma elish–type cosmogony), not pure linguistics; Childs: grammar allows both, but “theology of P excludes” preexistent-chaos reading to emphasize transcendence. Hamilton: theology alone is insufficient—lexical, grammatical, syntactical, comparative, and stylistic arguments also support “In the beginning.”
- **Quote:** “several scholars (e.g., Westermann) have opted for the traditional translation, not on the basis of objective linguistic grounds… but on the grounds of the wider context… deliberate repudiation and demythologizing of a pagan cosmogony such as is found in Enuma elish. … Brevard Childs says… “While there is a choice grammatically the theology of P excludes the latter possibility…” … one does not argue for the translation of 1:1 simply on the grounds of a biblical writer’s creation theology. … valid lexical, grammatical, syntactical, comparative, and stylistic arguments have been advanced to substantiate the translation In the beginning.”
- **Locus:** raw L2329–L2333 / Gen 1:1
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[creation-ex-nihilo]], [[genesis-ancient-near-east]], [[documentary-hypothesis]]

### C-V1R2-08
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Lexical support: Isa 46:9–10 uses *rēʾšîṯ* absolutely for God’s absolute disposition over beginning and end (historical time as such); *berēʾšîṯ* elsewhere (Jer 26:1 etc.) is followed by a noun, only Gen 1:1 by a finite perfect verb—different from 2:4b’s infinitive construct relative “when.”
- **Quote:** “Isa. 46:9-10—“ I am God . . . declaring the end [’aharîṯ] from the beginning [mērē’ šîṯ].” … beginning and end indicating not “a specific period of time within history, but rather historical time as such.” … Only in Gen. 1:1 is the noun followed by a verb in a finite form… Here contrast needs to be made with Gen. 2:4b… Everybody agrees that this is a relative sentence… But the noun in this verse is followed not by a verb in a finite form, as in 1:1, but by a verb in a nonfinite form…”
- **Locus:** raw L2335–L2337 / Gen 1:1; 2:4b
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[creation-ex-nihilo]], [[genesis-creation-accounts]]

### C-V1R2-09
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Absence of article is not fatal against absolute; all ancient versions translate absolute independent clause; Masoretes accented with disjunctive *ṭiphâ* (absolute), not conjunctive (construct).
- **Quote:** “The absence of the article is not a fatal argument against construing the word as absolute. … Second, all the ancient versions translate the word as an absolute and the whole verse as an independent clause. … Third, the Masoretes understood the word to be absolute, for they accented the word with the disjunctive accent called a ipḥâ…”
- **Locus:** raw L2339–L2339 / Gen 1:1
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[creation-ex-nihilo]], [[genesis]]

### C-V1R2-10
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Syntactically/comparatively: Enuma elish 1–9 is more like Gen 2:4bff. than Gen 1:1–3; if any parallel to 1:1–3, 1:2 // EE 1–8 and 1:3 // EE 9—Gen 1:1 is unique. Gunkel: other cosmogonies have “no word which would come close to the first word of the Bible.”
- **Quote:** “there is a syntactical similarity between Enuma elish 1-9 and Gen. 2:4bff., but not between Enuma elish 1-9 and Gen. 1:1-3. If there is any parallel… Gen. 1:2 parallels Enuma elish 1-8, and Gen. 1:3 parallels Enuma elish 9. Obviously Gen. 1:1 is unique. Gunkel was quite correct when he said, “The cosmogonies of other people contain no word which would come close to the first word of the Bible.””
- **Locus:** raw L2341–L2341 / Gen 1:1–3; 2:4b
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[genesis-ancient-near-east]], [[genesis-creation-accounts]], [[creation-ex-nihilo]]

### C-V1R2-11
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Stylistically, traditional translation fits chapter’s paratactic short sentences, not long subordinate+principal complexes; adverbial “initially/first” would more naturally be *bāriʾšōnâ*, not *berēʾšîṯ*.
- **Quote:** “On stylistic grounds the traditional translation conforms to the pattern of sentence lengths throughout the chapter. … brief, terse sentences in paratactic style. … the interpretation that takes the first verse… with adverbial force, “initially, first,” … such a nuance would be expressed more directly in Hebrew by the phrase bāri‘šōnâ…”
- **Locus:** raw L2343–L2345 / Gen 1:1
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[genesis]], [[creation-ex-nihilo]]

### C-V1R2-12
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** *tôhû wābōhû* are two rhyming nouns (“a desert and a wasteland”), not adjectives; *bōhû* only three times always with *tōhû*; *tōhû* (~20×) may stand alone; Ugaritic *thw* “desert”; nuances from parallels: desert, wilderness, wind, nothing, vanity.
- **Quote:** “Both these words are nouns, and thus we have translated them a desert and a wasteland. The rendering “without form and void” … might give the impression that the words are adjectives. … bōhû-appears only three times in the OT and always in conjunction with tōhû… tōhû appears twenty times… tōhû may be safely equated with Ugar. thw, “desert.” … the nuance of tōhû is brought out most clearly by words with which it appears in parallel: desert, wilderness, wind, nothing, vanity.”
- **Locus:** raw L2347–L2357 / Gen 1:2
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[genesis]], [[account-of-creation]], [[genesis-ancient-near-east]]

### C-V1R2-13
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Isa 45:18–19 is key for whether Yahweh did not create the earth “a chaos” or “to be a chaos”—relevant to gap/judgment readings of 1:2.
- **Quote:** “For our purposes Isa. 45:18-19 is most interesting: “Yahweh ... did not create it [the earth] a chaos ... I did not say ... ‘Look for me in chaos.’” … an issue is raised in the interpretation of Gen. 1:2 on the basis of whether Isa. 45:18 reads “Yahweh did not create the earth a chaos” or “Yahweh did not create the earth to be a chaos.””
- **Locus:** raw L2357–L2357 / Gen 1:2
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[genesis]], [[account-of-creation]]

### C-V1R2-14
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Gen 1 states God created light but not darkness; other OT traditions place darkness within God’s creative acts (Isa 45:7).
- **Quote:** “Although Gen. 1 states that God created light (v. 3), it does not say that he created darkness. … Other creation traditions within the OT do place darkness within the sphere of God’s creative acts. Compare Isa. 45:7, “I form light and I create darkness.””
- **Locus:** raw L2359–L2359 / Gen 1:2–3
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[genesis]], [[account-of-creation]]

### C-V1R2-15
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Even if *tehôm* ~ Tiamat etymologically, Gen 1’s deep is not personified or antagonistic; linguistic link more likely Ugaritic *thm* / Eblaite *ti-’a-matum*; primeval watery mass is widespread (Egypt Nu; Thales)—so Babylonian background is not demonstrated.
- **Quote:** “the deep of Gen. 1 is so far removed in function from the Tiamat of Enuma elish that any possible relationship is blurred beyond recognition. The deep of Gen. 1 is not personified, and in no way is it viewed as some turbulent, antagonistic force. … Much more likely is the correspondence between Heb. tehôm and Ugar. thm … or even earlier Eblaite ti-’a-matum, “ocean abyss.””
- **Locus:** raw L2361–L2369 / Gen 1:2
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[genesis-ancient-near-east]], [[genesis]], [[account-of-creation]]

### C-V1R2-16
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Rejects “awesome gale / mighty wind” for *rûaḥ ʾĕlōhîm*: none of 18 other OT uses means “mighty wind”; phrase unites world-building and tabernacle-building (Exod 31:3); superlative *ʾĕlōhîm* ambiguous and would oppose *ʾĕlōhîm* of 1:1, 3; unambiguous “great/stormy wind” phrases exist elsewhere.
- **Quote:** “none of the other eighteen occurrences of this phrase in the OT means anything like “mighty wind.” The next appearance… Exod. 31:3… This key phrase unites, via an intertextual allusion, world building and tabernacle building… if the author had intended to say “a mighty wind” he could have used unambiguous expressions such as rûaḥ geḏôlâ… or rûaḥ ṣe‘ārâ…”
- **Locus:** raw L2371–L2381 / Gen 1:2
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[genesis]], [[account-of-creation]]

### C-V1R2-17
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Preferable: “S/spirit” or “wind” of God. Orlinsky argues “wind” (against Philo-led “christianizing”); Hamilton finds wind-as-destructive inconsistent with beneficent hovering; if *rûaḥ* is beneficent, “S/spirit”; Hebrew cannot mark capital S—risk of imposing trinitarian concepts not necessarily present.
- **Quote:** “If the emphasis that Gen. 1:2 wishes to make is that the rûaḥ is a destructive force, then we must opt for “wind.” If the emphasis… is that the rûaḥ is a beneficent force, then we must opt for “S/spirit.” It seems clear that the latter option is the preferable one. … To translate “Spirit” runs the risk of superimposing trinitarian concepts on Gen. 1 that are not necessarily present.”
- **Locus:** raw L2381–L2393 / Gen 1:2
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[genesis]], [[account-of-creation]]

### C-V1R2-18
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** *meraḥepeṯ* “hovering”: rare; Deut 32:11 eagle watching/protecting (possibly Ugar. ǵyr “protect”); Ugaritic *rḥp* always with eagles (“soar”)—describes birds not winds; in Gen 1:2 spirit “watching over” formlessness and darkness, kept in check.
- **Quote:** “from the Ugaritic passages and from the Deuteronomy passage it appears that rāḥap describes the actions of birds, not winds. … In Gen. 1:2 is the rûaḥ “sweeping” over the waters or “watching over” the waters? If the latter, then “spirit” would be decidedly more accurate. Yes, there is a formlessness there, a forboding darkness, but all is kept in check and under control by the spirit of God.”
- **Locus:** raw L2395–L2401 / Gen 1:2
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[genesis]], [[genesis-ancient-near-east]]

### C-V1R2-19
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Rejects gap theory (v. 1 perfect creation; catastrophe; v. 2 “became” *tōhû*; re-creation from v. 3): sequential waw+subject+perfect would not be used; *hāyâ* in circumstantial clauses normally stative; *tōhû wābōhû* is not judgment/Sheol.
- **Quote:** “The first of these suggestions is popularly known as the gap theory. … “the earth had become....” … if the writer had intended v. 2 to be read as a sequence to v. 1, he would never have used the construction he did: waw consecutive plus subject plus verb (in the perfect). … we see here a reference to the situation prior to specific creation, a situation of formlessness but over which God’s spirit superintends.”
- **Locus:** raw L2403–L2413 / Gen 1:1–3
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[genesis]], [[account-of-creation]], [[creation-ex-nihilo]]

### C-V1R2-20
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Syntactically v. 2 is distinct from and prior to v. 3 (not concurrent with v. 3). Overall: v. 1 = opening superscription and summary, functional equivalent of *tôlĕdôt* colophon for other Genesis divisions; v. 2 = situation prior to detailed creation in vv. 3ff.; v. 2 generalizes what vv. 3–31 particularize (same generalization→particularization as days 1–3 // 4–6).
- **Quote:** “on syntactical grounds v. 2 be understood as distinct from and prior to v. 3. … v. 1 is an opening statement functioning both as a superscription and as a summary. As such, it is the functional equivalent to the colophon “these are the generations of,” which is the introductory sentence to each of the remaining major divisions of Genesis. Verse 2 then describes the situation prior to the detailed creation that is spelled out in vv. 3ff. … this same movement occurs in v. 2 (generalization) and vv. 3-31 (particularization).”
- **Locus:** raw L2415–L2419 / Gen 1:1–3
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[genesis]], [[toledot]], [[account-of-creation]], [[creation-ex-nihilo]]

### C-V1R2-21
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Day 1: light is *sine qua non*; only two narrated divine words *yehî ʾôr*; “and God said” introduces fiat/command speech; Vulg. *fiat lux* yields “creation by fiat.”
- **Quote:** “This first day of six days of divine activity produces the creation of light. This is quite natural, for the existence of light is the sine qua non for the creation of anything else. … Actually there are only two narrated words of God on this first day: yehî’ôr, “Let there be light. ” … It is the Vulg. translation of v. 3, fiat lux… that has given birth to the phrase “creation by fiat.” The emphasis is on creation by speech as command.”
- **Locus:** raw L2443–L2449 / Gen 1:3–5
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[genesis]], [[account-of-creation]]

### C-V1R2-22
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Four modes of creation stories: action, conflict, birth/self-reproduction, speech. Gen 1–2 lack conflict and birth modes; both use action and speech. Alleged contrast “word (1:1–2:3) vs action (2:4–31)” is not maintained—only light is strictly fiat; other days combine fiat + subsequent activity. Source critics use word/action (and divine names) to separate P (1:1–2:4a, late) and J (2:4bff., earlier).
- **Quote:** “All Creation stories… (1) through action… (2) through conflict… (3) through birth and self-reproduction; (4) through speech. Obviously the second and third are not found in Gen. 1 and 2… Worth pursuing is the interpretation that claims… contrast… creation by word and creation by action… (By the way, this difference is one of the criteria that source critics use to drive a wedge between these two chapters; they label 1: 1-2:4a as “Priestly” and therefore late, and 2:4bff. as “Yahwistic” and therefore earlier…) … the only item in Gen. 1 that is created by fiat, strictly speaking, is light…”
- **Locus:** raw L2449–L2453 / Gen 1–2
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[genesis-creation-accounts]], [[documentary-hypothesis]], [[genesis]]

### C-V1R2-23
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Separation assigns each part to its sphere (not “pull apart”); verb five times in ch. 1. Kapelrud’s exile-separation exhortation is “fanciful”; better contrast: creation separates toward order; sin separates toward disorder.
- **Quote:** “separated means here not to pull apart, but to assign each part to its respective sphere and slot. … Kapelrud makes the point that the proliferation of “separate” in Gen. 1 functions as a subtle exhortation to the exiles… This suggestion strikes us as more fanciful and imaginative than exegetical. If anything… separation that is wholesome and a separation that is malignant. In creation there is separation toward order… In sin and trespass there is a separation toward disorder…”
- **Locus:** raw L2455–L2459 / Gen 1:4
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[genesis]], [[account-of-creation]]

### C-V1R2-24
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** God’s first creation is time (vv. 3–5), second is space (vv. 6–10); story begins and ends (2:1–3) with time; sanctification of time (*qdš*, 2:3) precedes sanctification of space (next *qdš* Exod 3:5). Light exists three “days” without sun—anticipatory; not mere scientific ignorance.
- **Quote:** “God’s first creation is time (vv. 3-5). His second creation is space (w. 6-10). … Can it be without significance that this Creation story commences in the context of time and concludes (2:1-3) with a return to that category, a day of rest? … What the author states is that God caused the light to shine from a source other than the sun for the first three “day.””
- **Locus:** raw L2463–L2465 / Gen 1:3–5; 2:1–3
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[genesis]], [[sabbath]], [[account-of-creation]]

### C-V1R2-25
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Evening-before-morning refrain does not prove sunset-to-sunset reckoning; other OT evidence suggests day beginning at sunrise; refrain marks vacant time till morning, end of day and start of next work.
- **Quote:** “The fact that evening is placed before morning throughout this chapter is not a foolproof indication that the OT reckons a day from sunset to sunset. There is some evidence that strongly suggests that the day was considered to begin in the morning at sunrise. … this refrain in Genesis refers not to the computation of a day but rather to the “vacant time till the morning, the end of a day and the beginning of the next work.””
- **Locus:** raw L2467–L2467 / Gen 1:5
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[genesis]], [[sabbath]]

### C-V1R2-26
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Day 2 *rāqîaʿ* (“vault,” AV “firmament”): from *rāqaʿ* “spread out” (stretch tent / hammer metal). Separates waters above/below. Enuma elish: sky from half of Tiamat’s corpse with locks/guards—wide discrepancy from biblical vault. Evaluation formula missing on day 2 in MT (LXX adds artificially); vault preliminary to dry land (v. 10).
- **Quote:** “The word we have translated as vault is Heb. rāqîa’… The basic meaning of the noun is determined by a consideration of the verb rāqaʿ. Here the basic idea is “to spread out,” … In this myth, sky is made not only from preexisting material but specifically from one-half of the cadaver of an evil goddess. … Only in connection with this second day is the phrase “and God saw how beautiful it was” absent in the MT.”
- **Locus:** raw L2493–L2523 / Gen 1:6–8
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[genesis-ancient-near-east]], [[genesis]], [[account-of-creation]]

### C-V1R2-27
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Day 3: two jussives suggest concomitant concentration of waters and emergence of dry land; last divine naming—naming later delegated to man. Shift to geocentric focus (earth/vegetation). Eight creative acts in six days: days 3 and 6 have two works each (double evaluation). Vegetation: *dešeʾ* inclusive of plants and trees (seed external vs internal); *mîn* not restricted to “species.” Point (divine word) and process (self-perpetuation) both affirmed.
- **Quote:** “Perhaps the use of two jussives in v. 9 suggests that the two developments… be understood as concomitant events. … This is the last time, in the creation context, that God will name anything. … Gen. 1 describes eight creative acts by God over a six-day period. … Day three: two works: earth and vegetation… Day six: two works: land animals and man… this translation assumes… that deše’ , verdure, is an all-inclusive word… Heb. mîn iṣ broad enough to allow “species” as well as “genus, family, order.” … Here then is both point and process…”
- **Locus:** raw L2555–L2583 / Gen 1:9–13
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[genesis]], [[account-of-creation]], [[adam]]

### C-V1R2-28
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Day 4: progression from light in general to specific luminaries with threefold function (separate day/night; signs of seasons/days/years; illuminate earth)—repeated in reverse in vv. 17–18. Strong antimythical polemic: luminaries created to serve, not be served; avoids *šemeš*/*yārēaḥ* (divinity-laden names); order sun–moon–stars vs Enuma elish stars–moon–sun; stars almost afterthought.
- **Quote:** “Few commentators deny that this whole chapter has a strong antimythical thrust. … Gen. 1:14ff. is saying that these luminaries are not eternal; they are created, not to be served but to serve. … He uses the unusual expression the greater luminary instead of the normal word for sun—šemeš… lesser luminary instead of… yārēaḥ… deliberate attempt to reject out of hand any apotheosizing of the luminaries… the order… sun, moon, stars. This order contrasts with the order in Enuma elish, in which priority is given to the stars… the reference to the stars… is touched on so briefly and quite anticlimactically.”
- **Locus:** raw L2623–L2645 / Gen 1:14–19
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[genesis-ancient-near-east]], [[genesis]], [[account-of-creation]]

### C-V1R2-29
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Day 5 corresponds to day 2 habitats. *tannînim*: large marine creatures, not combatants; even if Ps 74, Isa 27, 51 and Ugaritic *tnn* use dragon/Yamm battle language, Gen 1 has no battle; reappearance of *bārāʾ* (only subject God; product never material) underlines creation of large creatures. Gen 1 could not be more antimythical.
- **Quote:** “Genesis 1 does not even hint of a battle. The tannînim are simply large creatures of the water and are created by God. Perhaps the reappearance in v. 21 of the verb create, not used since v. 1, underlines this point. This is a verb whose only subject in the OT is God, and whose accusative is always the product and never the material. … Gen. 1 could not be written with a more antimythical basis.”
- **Locus:** raw L2669–L2697 / Gen 1:20–23
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[genesis-ancient-near-east]], [[genesis]], [[account-of-creation]], [[creation-ex-nihilo]]

### C-V1R2-30
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** First divine speech to creatures (imperative): blessing precedes command; first blessing is fish and fowl (not man); essence of blessing is fertility/reproduction.
- **Quote:** “For the first time in the Creation narrative God speaks to somebody. … But God’s blessing precedes his commands. … The recipient of God’s first blessing in the Bible is not man—that must wait until v. 28—but fish and fowl. Quite evidently, the essence of God’s blessing is the capacity to be fertile, to reproduce oneself.”

## B. THE GARDEN OF EDEN AND ITS FIRST OCCUPANTS (2:4–25)

### C-V1R2-51
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** First of ten *ʾēlleh tôlĕdôt* formulas in Genesis; uniquely of heavens and earth (others of persons/narratives). Hamilton takes 2:4a as **superscription** beginning unit 2 (not subscription ending P’s 1:1–2:4a): elsewhere *tôlĕdôt* introduces what follows; Skinner: genitive always of progenitor not progeny—so 2:4a describes what heavens and earth generate, not process of 1:1–2:3. Dividing 2:4 to keep P-formula off J text is artificial; redactor-*deus-ex-machina* theories open to challenge.
- **Quote:** “We take the approach that 2:3 concludes the first unit of Genesis and 2:4a begins the second unit. … everywhere else in Genesis the tôleḏôṯ formula functions as a superscription to what follows. … the tôleḏôṯ formula is always followed by the genitive of the progenitor, never of the progeny. Thus the phrase the generations of the heavens and the earth describes not the process by which the heavens and the earth are generated, but rather that which is generated by the heavens and the earth. Quite obviously this would be a most inaccurate description of the process of creation as delineated in 1:1-2:3.”
